# Dataset explanation

This dataset was created using a fresh frozen eyeball issue sample from a mouse (Strain: C57BL/6; Sex: Male; Age: 6-8 week), using a Kit version Stereo-seq T FF V1.3 on a ship size : 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm with a section thickness of 10 μm and H&E staining. You can find more information [here](https://en.stomics.tech/col1251/index.html)

# Download dataset

Download the dataset from the [STOmics website](https://en.stomics.tech/col1251/index.html). The demo data has a different file structure than data coming from a real sequencing experiment. Once you have downloaded the demo dataset, please re-arrange the files to use the Giotto reader, your folder should look similar to this:

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="40%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Dataset file structure"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/0_file_structure.png")
```

# Set up Giotto environment

Ensure that the Giotto package is installed. Additionally, check that the mini conda Giotto environment with Python dependencies is installed.

If you have installation troubles, visit the [Installation](https://giotto-suite.github.io/Giotto_website/articles/installation.html) and [Frequently Asked Questions](https://giotto-suite.github.io/Giotto_website/articles/faqs.html) sections.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Ensure Giotto Suite is installed.
if(!"Giotto" %in% installed.packages()) {
  pak::pkg_install("giotto-suite/Giotto")
}

# Ensure the Python environment for Giotto has been installed.
genv_exists <- Giotto::checkGiottoEnvironment()
if(!genv_exists){
  # The following command need only be run once to install the Giotto environment.
  Giotto::installGiottoEnvironment()
}

library(Giotto)
```

# Set the Giotto instructions

{Giotto} instructions are used to apply settings to giotto object behavior at the project level. Each giotto object needs a set of instructions information that can either be manually set or generated with defaults when the giotto object is first created. Once added, these instructions are stored in the giotto object @instructions slot.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Set the results directory to save plots
results_folder <- "path/to/results"

# Optional: Specify the path to a Python executable within a conda or miniconda 
# environment. If set to NULL (default), the Python executable within the previously installed Giotto environment will be used.
python_path <- NULL # alternatively, "/local/python/path/python" if desired.

# Create Giotto Instructions
instructions <- createGiottoInstructions(save_dir = results_folder,
                                         save_plot = TRUE,
                                         show_plot = FALSE,
                                         return_plot = FALSE,
                                         python_path = python_path)
```

The stereo-seq readers will look for the standardized files organization from the STOmics technology in the data folder and will automatically load the expression and spatial information to create the Giotto object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
## provide a path to your sample data. It should point to the "outs" subfolder under your main data folder.
data_path <- "/path/to/outs/"
```

# Create the Giotto object using the reader

This step will read multiple components at the same time and will create a Giotto object. You can create multiple combinations of the data, e.g. the expression matrix and spatial locations only (by setting load_image = FALSE and load_mask = FALSE).

```{r, eval=FALSE}
reader_bin <- importStereoSeq(stereoseq_dir = data_path)

g <- reader_bin$create_gobject(
  load_expression = TRUE,
  load_spatlocs = TRUE,
  load_image = TRUE,
  load_mask = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  instructions = instructions)
```

Visualize the object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g,
           show_image = TRUE,
           point_size = 4)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of cells"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/0-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Read bin data using individual loaders

When reading the expression information at the bin level, you can select from different resolutions (e.g. "bin1", "bin5", "bin10", "bin20", "bin50", "bin100", "bin150", or "bin200").

## Start the reader for bin-level data

Some recommendations for using the reader:

 - Make sure to set: type = "bin".
 - The default bin size is "bin100", list the available bins in your sample with 'rhdf5::h5ls("/path/to/*.tissue.gef")'.
 - gene_column will determine if your features/genes use the common gene name (gene_column = "geneName") or an ENSEMBL id (gene_column = "geneID").
  - negative_y will control if the spatial y-coordinates are represented in the negative (negative_y = TRUE) or positive (negative_y = FALSE) space. You can see the difference when plotting your sample with `spatPlot2D()`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
reader_bin <- importStereoSeq(
  stereoseq_dir = data_path,
  type = "bin",
  bin_size = "bin100",
  gene_column = "geneName",
  negative_y = TRUE
)
```

## Load expression

The output of this step will be an exprObj with the raw expression matrix 
(feature/gene x bin). At this bin size, this dataset has 1309 bins and 26535 genes.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
expr_bin <- reader_bin$load_expression(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load spatial locations

The output of this step will be an spatLocsObj with the spatial coordinates of 
each bin.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatlocs_bin <- reader_bin$load_spatlocs(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load image

The output of this step will be a giottoLargeImage with the HE image.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
img_bin <- reader_bin$load_image(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load mask

The output of this step will be a giottoPolygon with the cell boundaries from the *HE_mask.tiff file.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
mask_poly <- reader_bin$load_mask(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Assemble the object

Use the individual pieces to create a custom Giotto object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- giotto()
g_bin <- setGiotto(g_bin, expr_bin, verbose = TRUE)
g_bin <- setGiotto(g_bin, spatlocs_bin, verbose = TRUE)
g_bin <- setGiotto(g_bin, mask_poly, verbose = TRUE)  
g_bin <- setGiotto(g_bin, img_bin, verbose = TRUE)
```

This object has the default instructions. You can set the instructions we defined at the beginning of the tutorial using the instructions() function.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
instructions(g_bin) <- instructions
```

Visualize the object

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g_bin,
           show_image = TRUE,
           point_size = 4)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of bin 100"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/1-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Read bin data using the convenience function

Read the bin expression matrix, spatial locations, image, and polygons in one step.

Use gef_type = "tissue" (default) to read only the bins that overlap with the tissue area.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- createGiottoStereoSeqObjectBin(
    stereoseq_dir = data_path,
    bin_size = "bin100",
    gef_type = "tissue",   
    load_image = TRUE,
    load_mask = TRUE,
    verbose = TRUE,
    instructions = instructions
  )
```

Visualize the bins.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g_bin, 
           show_image = TRUE, 
           point_size = 4)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of bin 100 using convenience function"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/2-spatPlot2D.png")
```

Use gef_type = "full" to read all the bins, including those out of the tissue area.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- createGiottoStereoSeqObjectBin(
    stereoseq_dir = data_path,
    bin_size = "bin100",
    gef_type = "full",   
    load_image = TRUE,
    load_mask = TRUE,
    verbose = TRUE,
    instructions = instructions
  )
```

Visualize the bins.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g_bin, 
           show_image = TRUE, 
           point_size = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of bin 100 using gef type argument"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/3-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Read cell data using individual loaders

## Start the reader for cell-level data

Some recommendations for using the reader:

 - Make sure to set: type = "cell".
 - No need to use the "bin" argument in this scenario.
 - gene_column will determine if your features/genes use the common gene name (gene_column = "geneName") or an ENSEMBL id (gene_column = "geneID").
  - negative_y will control if the spatial y-coordinates are represented in the negative (negative_y = TRUE) or positive (negative_y = FALSE) space. You can see the difference when plotting your sample with `spatPlot2D()`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
reader_cell <- importStereoSeq(
  stereoseq_dir = data_path,
  type = "cell",
  gene_column = "geneName",
  negative_y = TRUE
)
```

## Load expression

The output of this step will be an exprObj with the raw expression matrix 
(feature/gene x cell). At the cell size, this dataset has 7527 cells and 25646 genes.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
expr_cell <- reader_cell$load_expression(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load spatial locations

The output of this step will be an spatLocsObj with the spatial coordinates of each cell.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatlocs_cell <- reader_cell$load_spatlocs(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load image

The output of this step will be a giottoLargeImage with the HE image.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
img_cell <- reader_cell$load_image(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load cell border polygons

The output of this step is a giottoPolygon object with the cell polygons, result of the cell segmentation.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
poly <- reader_cell$load_polygons(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Assemble the object

Use the individual pieces to create a custom Giotto object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- giotto()
g_cell <- setGiotto(g_cell, expr_cell, verbose = TRUE)
g_cell <- setGiotto(g_cell, spatlocs_cell, verbose = TRUE)
g_cell <- setGiotto(g_cell, poly, verbose = TRUE)  
g_cell <- setGiotto(g_cell, img_cell, verbose = TRUE)
```

Set the Giotto instructions

```{r, eval=FALSE}
instructions(g_cell) <- instructions
```

Visualize the object

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g_cell,
           show_image = TRUE,
           point_size = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of cells"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/4-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Read cell data using the convenience function

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- createGiottoStereoSeqObjectCell(
    stereoseq_dir = data_path,
    gef_type = "adjusted_cellbin",  # default
    load_polygons = TRUE,
    load_mask = FALSE,
    load_image = TRUE,
    verbose = TRUE,
    negative_y = TRUE,
    instructions = instructions
  )
```

Visualize the object

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(g_cell,
           show_image = TRUE,
           point_size = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of cells using the convenience function"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/5-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Read subcellular data using individual loaders

## Load subcellular bin data as binpoints

Read the smallest bin size (bin1) and create a giottoBinPoints object.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gbp_bin <- reader_bin$load_binpoints(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load mask polygons

The output of this step is a giottoPolygon object. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
mask_poly <- reader_bin$load_mask(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Load image

The output of this step will be a giottoLargeImage with the HE image.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
img_bin <- reader_bin$load_image(verbose = TRUE)
```

## Assemble the object

The resulting object will only contain subcellular data. The aggregated matrix can be calculated using downstream steps. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- giotto()
g_sub <- setGiotto(g_sub, gbp_bin, verbose = TRUE)
g_sub <- setGiotto(g_sub, mask_poly, verbose = TRUE)
g_sub <- setGiotto(g_sub, img_cell, verbose = TRUE)
```

Print the object and note there's only feature data in the subcellular info, but the aggregated info only contains the image.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Overlap the subcellular info with the cell segmentation polygons  to create an aggregated expression matrix.

Find the feature points overlapped by polygons. This overlap information is then returned to the relevant giottoPolygon object's overlaps slot.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- calculateOverlap(
  g_sub,
  spat_info = "cell",
  feat_info = "rna"
)
```

Convert the overlap information into a cell by feature expression matrix which is then stored in the Giotto object's expression slot.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- overlapToMatrix(
  g_sub,
  spat_info = "cell",
  feat_info = "rna",
  name = "raw"
)
```

Print the object again and note the aggregated info with raw counts.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Set the Giotto instructions and visualize the aggregated object at the cell level. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
instructions(g_sub) <- instructions

spatPlot2D(g_sub,
           show_image = TRUE,
           point_size = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of aggregated cells"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/6-spatPlot2D.png")
```

# Create a Giotto object using subcellular and cell segmentation data

Read both the mask and giottoBinPoints in a single step, then run a second step to aggregate the data at the cell-level expression matrix.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- reader_bin$create_gobject(
  load_expression = FALSE,
  load_spatlocs = FALSE,
  load_image = TRUE,
  load_mask = TRUE,
  load_binpoints = TRUE,
  verbose = TRUE,
  instructions = instructions)
```

Print the object and note there's only subcellular info.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Calculate the overlap with cell polygons and the aggregated matrix.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- calculateOverlap(
  g_sub,
  spat_info = "cell",
  feat_info = "rna"
)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- overlapToMatrix(
  g_sub,
  spat_info = "cell",
  feat_info = "rna",
  name = "raw"
)
```

Print the object again and note the aggregated info with raw counts.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Visualize the cell polygons and some genes. You can select genes to plot their location across the sample. spatInSituPlotPoints will also plot the segmentation cell boundaries stored as Giotto Polygons. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
genes <- featIDs(g_sub)
selected_genes <- genes[sample(size = 100, x = 1:length(genes))]

spatInSituPlotPoints(
  gobject = g_sub,
  show_image = TRUE,
  image_name = "image",
  show_polygon = TRUE,
  polygon_feat_type = "cell",
  polygon_color = "white",
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_line_size = 0.3,
  feats = list('rna' = selected_genes),
  use_overlap = FALSE,
  show_legend = FALSE,
  spat_unit = "cell",
  point_size = 0.3
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial locations of some sampled transcripts"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/7-spatInSituPlotPoints.png")
```

# Read subcellular data using the convenience function

When using createGiottoStereoSeqObjectBin(), load_binpoints = TRUE will read the smallest resolution bin (bin1) as giottoBinPoints, while load_mask = TRUE will load the cell polygons. This information will be used in a downstream step to aggregate the bin1 counts at the cellular level.

Optionally, you can also read the expression matrix at any bin resolution. In this example, we are also loading the bin1 expression by setting bin_size = "bin1" and load_expression = TRUE. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- createGiottoStereoSeqObjectBin(
    stereoseq_dir = data_path,
    bin_size = "bin1", # smallest resolution expression matrix
    gef_type = "tissue",
    load_expression = TRUE, # bin1 expression matrix
    load_spatlocs = TRUE,
    load_binpoints = TRUE, # bin1 giottoBinPoints (0.5 µm DNBs)
    load_image = TRUE,
    load_mask = TRUE, # cell polygons from HE mask
    verbose = TRUE,
    instructions = instructions
  )
```

Print the object and note that the aggregated info only contains the bin1 level, but not cellular level.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Overlap the giottoBinPoints and cell polygons.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub <- calculateOverlap(
    g_sub,
    spat_info = "cell",
    feat_info = "rna"
  )

g_sub <- overlapToMatrix(
    g_sub,
    spat_info = "cell",
    feat_info = "rna",
    name = "raw"
  )
```

Print the object again and note that the aggregated info now contains both the bin1 and cellular level.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_sub
```

Visualize the cell polygons and some genes.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatInSituPlotPoints(g_sub,
                     spat_unit = "cell",
                     show_image = FALSE,
                     show_polygon = TRUE,
                     polygon_feat_type = "cell",
                     polygon_color = "white",
                     polygon_alpha = 0,
                     polygon_line_size = 0.2,
                     feats = list("rna" = c("Slc4a11", "Myh7", "Mylk4")),
                     feats_color_code = c("Slc4a11" = "yellow",
                                          "Myh7" = "green",
                                          "Mylk4" = "red"),
                     point_size = 0.3,
                     use_overlap = FALSE,
                     show_legend = FALSE,
                     background_color = "black"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial locations of Slc4a11, Myh7 and Mylk4 transcripts"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/8-spatInSituPlotPoints.png")
```

Use subsetGiottoLocsSubcellular to subset a specific region of the sample and obtain a zoomed in visualization of the transcripts.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_subset <- subsetGiottoLocs(g_sub,
                             spat_unit = "cell",
                             x_min = 2750,
                             x_max = 3100,
                             y_min = -9000,
                             y_max = -8500)

spatInSituPlotPoints(g_subset,
                     spat_unit = "cell",
                     show_image = FALSE,
                     show_polygon = TRUE,
                     polygon_feat_type = "cell",
                     polygon_color = "white",
                     polygon_alpha = 0,
                     polygon_line_size = 0.2,
                     feats = list("rna" = c("Myh7", "Mylk4")),
                     feats_color_code = c("Myh7" = "green",
                                          "Mylk4" = "red"),
                     expand_counts = TRUE,
                     count_info_column = "count",
                     jitter = c(1, 1),
                     point_size = 1,
                     use_overlap = FALSE,
                     background_color = "black"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial locations of Myh7 and Mylk4 transcripts in a subset object"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/9-spatInSituPlotPoints.png")
```

# Process the Giotto object at the cell level

## Quality control

Use the function addStatistics() to count the number of features per cell. The statistics information will be stored in the metadata table under the new column “nr_feats”. Then, use this column to visualize the number of features per cell across the sample.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_statistics <- addStatistics(gobject = g_cell,
                              expression_values = "raw")

## visualize
spatPlot2D(gobject = g_statistics, 
           point_size = 2,
           cell_color = "nr_feats", 
           color_as_factor = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of features per cell."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/10-spatPlot2D.png")
```

filterDistributions() creates a histogram to show the distribution of features per cell across the sample.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
filterDistributions(gobject = g_statistics, 
                    detection = "cells")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Distribution of features per cell."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/11-filterDistributions.png")
```

When setting the detection = "feats", the histogram shows the distribution of cells with certain number of features across the sample.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
filterDistributions(gobject = g_statistics, 
                    detection = "feats")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Distribution of cells with different features per cell."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/12-filterDistributions.png")
```

## Filtering

Use the arguments feat_det_in_min_cells and min_det_feats_per_cell to set the minimal number of cells where an individual feature must be detected and the minimal number of features per cell, respectively, to filter the giotto object. All the features and cells under those thresholds will be removed from the sample.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- filterGiotto(gobject = g_cell,
                       expression_threshold = 1,
                       feat_det_in_min_cells = 10,
                       min_det_feats_per_cell = 100,
                       expression_values = "raw",
                       verbose = TRUE)
```

## Normalization

Use scalefactor to set the scale factor to use after library size normalization. The default value is 6000, but you can use a different one.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- normalizeGiotto(gobject = g_cell, 
                          scalefactor = 6000, 
                          verbose = TRUE)
```

Calculate the normalized number of features per cell and save the statistics in the metadata table.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- addStatistics(gobject = g_cell)

## visualize
spatPlot2D(gobject = g_cell, 
           point_size = 2,
           show_image = TRUE, 
           point_alpha = 0.7,
           cell_color = "nr_feats", 
           color_as_factor = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of the number of features per cell."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/13-spatPlot2D.png")
```

You can also visualize the number of transcripts per cell.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(gobject = g_cell, 
           point_size = 2,
           show_image = TRUE, 
           point_alpha = 0.7,
           cell_color = "total_expr", 
           color_as_factor = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial distribution of the number of transcripts per cell."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/14-spatPlot2D.png")
```

## Feature selection

Calculating Highly Variable Features (HVF) is necessary to identify genes (or features) that display significant variability across the cells. 

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- calculateHVF(gobject = g_cell, 
                       save_plot = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Covariance of HVFs using the binned method."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/15-HVFplot.png")
```

## Dimension reduction

### PCA

Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is applied to reduce the dimensionality of gene expression data by transforming it into principal components, which are linear combinations of genes ranked by the variance they explain, with the first components capturing the most variance.

- runPCA() will look for the previous calculation of highly variable features, stored as a column in the feature metadata. If the HVF labels are not found in the giotto object, or the parameter "feats_to_use" is set to NULL, then runPCA() will use all the features available in the sample to calculate the Principal Components.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- runPCA(gobject = g_cell,
                 ncp = 50)
```

Create a screeplot to visualize the percentage of variance explained by each component.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
screePlot(gobject = g_cell, 
          ncp = 50)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Screeplot showing the variance explained per principal component."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/16-screePlot.png")
```

- Visualize the PCA calculated using the HVFs.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plotPCA(gobject = g_cell)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="PCA plot using HVFs."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/17-PCA.png")
```

### UMAP

Unlike PCA, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and t-Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) do not assume linearity. After running PCA, UMAP or t-SNE allows you to visualize the dataset in 2D.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
## run UMAP on PCA space (default)
g_cell <- runUMAP(g_cell, 
                  dimensions_to_use = 1:10)

plotUMAP(gobject = g_cell)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="UMAP using the 10 first principal components."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/18-UMAP.png")
```

### tSNE

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- runtSNE(g_cell, 
                  dimensions_to_use = 1:10,
                  check_duplicates = FALSE)

plotTSNE(gobject = g_cell)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="tSNE using the 10 first principal components."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/19-tSNE.png")
```

## Clustering

### Calculate the nearest neighbors

In preparation for the clustering calculation, finding the cells with similar expression patterns is needed. There are two methods available in Giotto:

- Create a sNN network (default)

The shared Nearest Neighbor algorithm defines the similarity between a pair of points in terms of their shared nearest neighbors. That is, the similarity between two points is "confirmed" by their common (shared) near neighbors. If point A is close to point B and if they are both close to a set of points C then we can say that A and B are close with greater confidence since their similarity is "confirmed" by the points in set C. You can find more information about this method [here](https://d1wqtxts1xzle7.cloudfront.net/67759720/siam_hd_snn_cluster-libre.pdf?1624717643=&response-content-disposition=inline%3B+filename%3DA_new_shared_nearest_neighbor_clustering.pdf&Expires=1744241905&Signature=EKZIFpKKGUPYegDxxL58WDtO6UhM9suqxSvauIzd8SWExXv5SPbhSgnvsnbMTOSWy56Vk-gyQUgazWCfh~lRg65CIZQqFStuNptUdIB4RvnWFJPT2jYfLgojTpDBKWLX8fn3Ab-sPxlUaqPV5m9E6WCunZqlQMNClLTKOK6L4D5NJs2XJl5u7bHGfHuMCLzPLLzBBfB-QLWDrXvhBmpX1ZOcX0O1YcOD1aNyQ2bCjNdCKRlSEMtX2Cboxe7B-Xf5bKRlA31JDTC~MUn3JGxHuDKpFKlwCZss980SIb1dbNz0vULD86nO6qIYbS1oQRIJHG260jox5s65TCJvO8rRIA__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAJLOHF5GGSLRBV4ZA). By default, createNearestNetwork() calculates 30 shared Nearest Neighbors for each cell, but you can modify this number using the "k" parameter.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- createNearestNetwork(gobject = g_cell, 
                               dimensions_to_use = 1:10)
```

- Create a kNN network

The K-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm operates on the principle of likelihood of similarity. It posits that similar data points tend to cluster near each other in space. You can find more information about this method [here.](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-024-00973-y) By default, createNearestNetwork() finds the 30 K-Nearest Neighbors to each cell, but you can modify this number using the "k" parameter.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- createNearestNetwork(gobject = g_cell, 
                               dimensions_to_use = 1:10, 
                               type = "kNN")
```

### Leiden clustering

This algorithm is more complicated than the Louvain algorithm and have an accurate and fast result for the computation time. The Leiden algorithm consists of three phases. The first phase is the modularity optimization process, the second phase is the refinement of partition, and the third phase is the community aggregation process. This algorithm performs well on small, medium and large-scale networks. You can find more information about Louvain and Leiden clustering [here](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/2129/1/012028/pdf)

- Run the Leiden clustering algorithm.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_cell <- doLeidenCluster(gobject = g_cell, 
                          resolution = 1)
```

- Plot dimension and spatial plots using the Leiden clusters information.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plotPCA(gobject = g_cell,
        cell_color = "leiden_clus")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="PCA plot, colors indicate the Leiden clusters."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/20-PCA.png")
```

Set the argument "show_NN_network = TRUE" to visualize the connections between spots.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plotUMAP(gobject = g_cell,
         cell_color = "leiden_clus", 
         show_NN_network = TRUE, 
         point_size = 1.5)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="UMAP plot, colors indicate the Leiden clusters."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/21-UMAP.png")
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plotTSNE(gobject = g_cell,
         cell_color = "leiden_clus")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="UMAP plot, colors indicate the Leiden clusters."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/22-tSNE.png")
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(gobject = g_cell, 
           point_size = 1,
           show_image = FALSE, 
           background_color = "black",
           cell_color = "leiden_clus")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial plot, colors indicate the Leiden clusters."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/23-spatPlot2D.png")
```


# Process the Giotto object at the bin level

To follow this portion of the tutorial, use the bin100 object that only contains the features overlapping with the tissue. See the section "Read bin data using the convenience function".

- Filtering

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- filterGiotto(gobject = g_bin,
                      expression_threshold = 1,
                      feat_det_in_min_cells = 10,
                      min_det_feats_per_cell = 50,
                      expression_values = "raw",
                      verbose = TRUE)
```

- Normalization

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- normalizeGiotto(gobject = g_bin, 
                         scalefactor = 6000, 
                         verbose = TRUE)
```

- Feature selection

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- calculateHVF(gobject = g_bin, 
                      save_plot = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Covariance of HVFs using the binned method"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/24-HVFplot.png")
```

- Dimension reduction

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- runPCA(gobject = g_bin,
                ncp = 50)

g_bin <- runUMAP(g_bin, 
                 dimensions_to_use = 1:10)

g_bin <- runtSNE(g_bin, 
                 dimensions_to_use = 1:10,
                 check_duplicates = FALSE)
```

- Create Nearest network

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- createNearestNetwork(gobject = g_bin, 
                              dimensions_to_use = 1:10)
```

- Run the Leiden clustering algorithm.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g_bin <- doLeidenCluster(gobject = g_bin, 
                         resolution = 1)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
plotUMAP(gobject = g_bin,
         cell_color = "leiden_clus", 
         show_NN_network = TRUE, 
         point_size = 1.5)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="UMAP using the 10 first principal components. Bin spots are colored by Leiden cluster"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/25-UMAP.png")
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spatPlot2D(gobject = g_bin, 
           point_size = 4,
           show_image = FALSE, 
           point_alpha = 0.7,
           background_color = "black",
           cell_color = "leiden_clus")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="60%", fig.align="center", fig.alt="Spatial plot, colors indicate the Leiden clusters"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stereoseq_mouse_eyeball/26-spatPlot2D.png")
```
